faq.q: Can a single negative IHA rule out disease?

faq.a: Most labs use ≥1:20 as the cut‑off, but a titre ≥1:160 in a symptomatic patient strongly supports invasive disease.
Yes; a four‑fold fall in titre over weeks indicates effective therapy.
faq.q: Is IHA useful for monitoring treatment?

exam: What is the principle behind indirect haemagglutination and why is it preferred over direct HA for melioidosis? — Antibody‑mediated agglutination of antigen‑coated RBCs; indirect HA detects patient antibodies, direct HA detects antigen on cells.
A patient with fever and liver abscess has a negative IHA today. What is your next step? — Repeat IHA in 7 days or obtain culture/aspirate because early serology may be false‑negative.

How would you differentiate brucellosis from typhoid when both give a positive IHA? — Look at clinical pattern (arthralgia, occupational exposure) and use specific Brucella agglutination titres; typhoid serology uses Widal.
Why is doxycycline‑rifampicin combination preferred for brucellosis over monotherapy? — Synergy reduces relapse; monotherapy leads to persistent intracellular organisms.
A patient’s IHA titre falls from 1:320 to 1:80 after two weeks of therapy. What does this indicate? — Good serological response, likely clinical improvement.
What red‑flag sign would prompt urgent referral in a patient being investigated with IHA for leptospirosis? — Development of hypotension, oliguria, or pulmonary hemorrhage.
If the laboratory lacks IHA reagents, what alternative test can you request for suspected melioidosis? — PCR for B. pseudomallei or culture on Ashdown’s medium.

Explain why a high IHA titre may be seen in an asymptomatic carrier of Brucella and how you would manage it. — Chronic low‑level exposure maintains antibodies; treat only if symptomatic or occupational risk high.
ai.title: Indirect Haemagglutination Test
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: The indirect haemagglutination (IHA) test detects antibodies against specific pathogens by agglutinating antigen‑coated red cells. It is highly sensitive for invasive infections such as melioidosis and brucellosis, but may be negative early or in asymptomatic carriers.

b: Positive result: agglutination at ≥1:20 dilution (lab‑specific cut‑off).
Negative result: no agglutination at the highest dilution tested.
sections.p: IHA is a serological assay in which patient serum is mixed with red blood cells coated with purified antigen. Antibody binding causes visible clumping (agglutination).

b: Acute invasive disease: high titre (≥1:160) with systemic signs.
Convalescent phase: falling titre, clinical improvement.
sections.p: IHA does not stage disease; clinical severity is judged by organ involvement, vital signs and imaging. Serial titres can indicate response – a four‑fold fall suggests cure.

b: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) – common in East Africa’s wet zones.
Brucellosis – occupational exposure to livestock.
Leptospirosis – exposure to contaminated water.
Rickettsial infections – tick‑borne fevers.
sections.p: IHA is used for pathogens that elicit strong IgG responses and where culture is difficult.

b: Fever >38 °C for >5 days.
Weight loss, night sweats.
Localized pain or abscess formation.
sections.p: Patients typically have fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and organ‑specific signs (e.g., lung infiltrates in melioidosis, arthritis in brucellosis).

t.b: Does the patient have antibodies to the suspected pathogen? – Positive titre supports invasive disease; negative does not exclude early infection.
Is the organism recoverable? – Positive culture confirms diagnosis; helps guide antibiotics.
What is the systemic response? – Leukocytosis or transaminase rise indicates severity.

b: Persistent fever >7 days despite antibiotics.
Rapidly rising IHA titre (>four‑fold in 48 h).
Signs of organ failure: hypotension, altered mental status, respiratory distress.
sections.p: Unchecked invasive infection can lead to septic shock, organ abscesses, and death.

b: Melioidosis – high‑dose IV ceftazidime or meropenem for 2 weeks, then oral trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for 3‑6 months.
Brucellosis – doxycycline + rifampicin for 6 weeks; avoid monotherapy to prevent relapse.
Leptospirosis – IV penicillin G or doxycycline; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.
Supportive care – fluids, oxygen, treat organ‑specific complications.
sections.p: Treat the underlying infection; IHA guides choice and duration.

b: Vaccination where available (e.g., Brucella in high‑risk workers).
Protective footwear and gloves for farmers.
Safe water and sanitation to reduce leptospirosis.
sections.p: Repeat IHA after 2–4 weeks to document falling titre; educate on exposure avoidance.

b: Direct HA – used for blood‑group typing, not antibody detection.
ELISA – more quantitative, but requires equipment often lacking in low‑resource labs.
sections.p: Direct haemagglutination (detects antigen on patient cells) and ELISA (enzyme‑linked detection).

b: Prior exposure to related organisms (e.g., other Burkholderia species) can raise baseline titre.
Immunosuppressed patients may not mount detectable antibodies.
sections.p: Cross‑reactive antibodies may cause false‑positive titres; early infection may be seronegative.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever despite appropriate antibiotics
